rooms.about: English 9 introduces the major genres of literature, including the short story, poetry, drama, the epic and the novel, alongside nonfiction and rhetoric. You will write analytical, argumentative and narrative essays, conduct research, and refine grammar and style.

units.t: Reading Like a Writer: Literary Analysis
learn: Literary analysis examines how an author creates meaning, not just what happens. The key question is always how and why: how does this choice of detail, structure or language shape the reader’s understanding?
Annotation is active reading on the page. Mark repeated words and images, shifts in tone, surprising choices and questions. Patterns you notice often become the basis of a thesis.

An analytical thesis is arguable and specific. Weak: “The story uses symbolism.” Strong: “By returning to the image of the locked gate, the author suggests that the narrator’s isolation is self-imposed.”

Body paragraphs follow a pattern: topic sentence, context, embedded quotation, and commentary that explains how the evidence supports the claim. Commentary should be at least as long as the quotation.
units.try: Choose a short story you know. Annotate one page for repeated images. Write a one-sentence thesis that names the author’s technique and its effect, then draft one body paragraph with a topic sentence, an embedded quotation and two sentences of commentary.
check: The recurring storm imagery mirrors the family’s growing conflict
The story has a storm in it
I liked the story because it was exciting
In a body paragraph, commentary should
Explain how the evidence supports the claim
Repeat the quotation in other words only

units.t: The Short Story: Plot, Character and Point of View
learn: Plot structure often follows exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution. Authors may disrupt chronology with flashback (a return to earlier events) or foreshadowing (hints of what is to come).
Complex characters have conflicting motivations and develop over the story. A foil is a character whose contrasting traits highlight those of another.

Point of view shapes what we know. First person is limited to the narrator’s perspective; third-person limited follows one character’s thoughts; third-person omniscient can reveal any character’s mind.
Conflict can be internal (a character struggling with a choice) or external (character versus another character, society, nature or technology).
units.try: Rewrite a key paragraph of a story you have read from a different point of view, such as changing first person to third-person omniscient. Then write three sentences explaining what the reader learns or loses because of the change.

A hint about what will happen later in a story is called

learn: A symbol is a concrete object, character or event that also represents an abstract idea. A light that a character reaches for might represent hope or an unreachable dream.
Setting is more than time and place; it can create mood, reflect a character’s inner state or reveal social pressures. A cramped, dark apartment might reinforce a feeling of being trapped.
Themes are complex statements about human experience. A text can develop several, and strong readers trace how a theme emerges, is shaped by details and is refined over the course of the work.
Avoid clichés or commands when stating themes. Instead of “Never give up,” write “Persistence can become harmful when it blinds a person to changing circumstances.”
units.try: Choose an object that appears more than once in a story or film you know. List each appearance and what is happening at the time. Write a paragraph arguing what the object symbolizes and how its meaning changes.
check: What is a symbol in literature?
A concrete thing that represents an abstract idea
A list of the setting’s details
Which is the best statement of a theme?
Ambition can isolate people from those who care about them

units.t: Poetry: Imagery, Figurative Language and Form
learn: Imagery appeals to the senses. Diction is word choice, and syntax is word order; both shape tone. A poem’s speaker is the voice in the poem and is not necessarily the poet.
Extended metaphors carry one comparison through a whole poem. Apostrophe directly addresses an absent person, object or idea, as in “O Death.”

Forms include the Shakespearean sonnet (14 lines, ABAB CDCD EFEF GG, ending in a couplet), the villanelle (19 lines with two repeating refrains) and free verse. Enjambment lets a sentence run past a line break; a caesura is a pause within a line.
A shift, or volta, is a turn in thought or tone, often signaled by words like but or yet. Analyzing a poem means connecting its devices to its meaning.
units.try: Read a sonnet aloud. Mark its rhyme scheme with letters, circle the volta, and write two sentences explaining how the final couplet answers or changes the earlier lines.
check: What is the rhyme scheme of the final two lines of a Shakespearean sonnet?
When a sentence continues past the end of a poetic line, it is called

learn: Shakespeare (1564 to 1616) wrote about 37 plays. Romeo and Juliet, a tragedy set in Verona, follows two young lovers from feuding families. A tragedy ends in catastrophe, often caused by a mix of fate and human choices.
Shakespeare wrote mostly in blank verse, unrhymed iambic pentameter, with ten syllables per line in a da-DUM pattern. Servants and comic scenes often use prose.
The prologue is a sonnet that tells the audience the ending: the “star-crossed lovers” will die. This creates dramatic irony throughout the play.
Key ideas include the haste of youth, the destructiveness of hatred and the conflict between love and family loyalty. Archaic words: wherefore means why, and thou means you.
units.try: Read Juliet’s balcony lines that begin “O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?” Paraphrase the speech in modern English. Then explain why “wherefore” here asks why he is a Montague, not where he is.
check: What does “wherefore” mean in Shakespeare’s English?

learn: An epic is a long narrative poem about a hero whose journey reflects the values of a culture. The Odyssey, attributed to Homer and composed around the 700s BCE in ancient Greece, follows Odysseus’s ten-year journey home after the Trojan War.
Epic conventions include beginning in medias res (in the middle of the action), invoking a Muse, epic similes (long, detailed comparisons) and epithets like “gray-eyed Athena.”
Odysseus faces the Cyclops, the Sirens and Scylla and Charybdis. He is clever but also proud; his boast to the Cyclops brings the god Poseidon’s anger.
The hero’s journey pattern includes a call to adventure, trials, a descent or lowest point, transformation and return. Themes include hospitality (xenia), loyalty and the cost of pride.
units.try: Map Odysseus’s journey (or a modern hero’s journey from a film) onto the stages: call, trials, lowest point, transformation, return. For each stage, write one event and what it reveals about the hero’s character.
check: What does in medias res mean?
Starting in the middle of the action
Which flaw causes Odysseus serious trouble with Poseidon?
His pride when boasting to the Cyclops

learn: Rhetoric is the art of persuasion. Aristotle described three appeals: ethos (credibility), pathos (emotion) and logos (logic and evidence). Kairos refers to the timing of an argument.
Rhetorical devices include repetition, parallelism (similar grammatical structure), rhetorical questions, antithesis (contrasting ideas side by side) and allusion.
The rhetorical situation includes the speaker, audience, purpose, context and message. Analyzing a speech means explaining how choices fit that situation.
Logical fallacies weaken arguments. Ad hominem attacks the person, a straw man misrepresents the opposing view, and a false dilemma presents only two options when more exist.
units.try: Read or listen to a famous speech, such as Martin Luther King Jr.’s “I Have a Dream” (1963). Find one example each of ethos, pathos and logos, and one use of repetition. Explain how each would affect the audience of that time.
check: An appeal to the audience’s emotions is
“Either we ban phones or students will never learn” is an example of

learn: An argument makes a precise claim, supports it with valid reasoning and sufficient evidence, and addresses counterclaims fairly. Evidence can include statistics, expert testimony, examples and reasoning.
Distinguish your claim from alternate claims, and explain the limitations of each side. A concession admits a valid point before a rebuttal shows why your claim is stronger overall.
Organize logically: introduction with context and thesis, body paragraphs each with one reason, a counterargument paragraph, and a conclusion that extends the significance.
Maintain a formal, objective tone. Use varied transitions to show relationships: consequently (cause), nevertheless (contrast), similarly (comparison), in particular (example).
units.try: Outline an essay on “Should high school students be required to complete community service?” Write a thesis, three reasons each with a type of evidence you would use, one counterargument, and a concession-and-rebuttal sentence.
check: What is a concession in an argument?
Admitting a valid point of the opposing side
Restating your thesis word for word

learn: Phrases and clauses add variety. An independent clause can stand alone; a dependent clause cannot (“because it rained”). Combine them to make complex sentences.
A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses: “The bell rang; nobody moved.” A colon introduces a list, explanation or quotation after a complete sentence.
Parallel structure keeps items in the same form: “She likes hiking, swimming and reading,” not “hiking, to swim and reads.”
Avoid run-ons and comma splices (two sentences joined with only a comma). Fix them with a period, a semicolon or a comma plus a conjunction like and, but or so.
units.try:
Fix these sentences.
1. I finished the essay, I submitted it. → I finished the essay; I submitted it.
2. He wanted to run, jumping and to swim. → He wanted to run, jump and swim.
Then write two original sentences: one with a semicolon and one with a colon before a list.
check: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
The storm passed; the sky cleared
Two sentences joined with only a comma form a

learn: Novels develop complex themes across many chapters. Commonly studied ninth-grade novels include To Kill a Mockingbird by Harper Lee, Of Mice and Men by John Steinbeck and Animal Farm by George Orwell. Track characters, conflicts and motifs (repeated ideas) as you read.
Research writing begins with a question narrow enough to answer. Gather information from multiple authoritative print and digital sources and assess each for accuracy, bias and usefulness.

Integrate sources smoothly with signal phrases (“According to historian…”), avoid over-relying on one source, and cite them using a standard format such as MLA, which uses in-text citations like (Lee 47) and a Works Cited list.
Connecting literature with research deepens understanding, for example researching the Great Depression to understand Of Mice and Men.
